implementation_notes: The standard library puts map directly on the types: map on Iterable/Collection is eager and returns a List<R> built from the transform lambda (the documentation's collection transformation operations), the same operator names on Sequence are lazy and single-use, and Result<T>.map transforms the success value while a failure passes through. Nullable values use ?.let or an explicit branch instead of a built-in optional context. There is no Functor typeclass in Kotlin and the ecosystem has moved away from one: Arrow 2.x removed the Functor/Applicative/Monad hierarchy because Kotlin cannot express higher-kinded types, exposing map as extension functions on Option/Either instead. That leaves extension functions with a shared name as the realization; a hand-written typeclass is justified only for an existing library dependency, not as new code.
code_sketch:
val names: List<String> = people.map { it.displayName }     // eager List

val some = people.asSequence()
    .map { it.displayName }                                  // lazy, single-use
    .take(5)
    .toList()

val port = runCatching { readPort(cfg) }.map { it.coerceAtLeast(1) }
pitfalls: Collection map is eager (one intermediate list per stage) while Sequence map is lazy and single-use: mixing them changes cost and semantics, and a sequence stage without a terminal operation does nothing.

?.let { f(it) } looks like map for nullable values but drops the receiver instead of preserving context: the result is not 'null stays null', so type the nullable explicitly when the distinction matters.

map drops nothing: a lambda returning null produces a List<T?>, while dropping nulls is mapNotNull and transforming map entries is mapValues/mapKeys - three operations that are easy to confuse with map.

variants.name: Flow.map (map inside an asynchronous, cold stream)
variants.implementation_notes: The asynchronous context maps with the same operator name: Flow<T>.map applies a suspend transform to each emitted value and returns a new cold flow, so mapping composes into a stream pipeline where nothing runs until a terminal operator (collect, toList, fold) starts collection - the coroutines documentation lists map among the intermediate operators that return another flow, and shows a hand-written equivalent built with flow {} and emit. Cancellation propagates through the transform, and backpressure/buffering operators sit on the same chain, which the collection and sequence forms cannot express. Prefer it when values arrive asynchronously; keep the suspend-free forms for in-memory data.
variants.code_sketch:
val emails: Flow<String> = peopleFlow
    .map { it.email }            // intermediate: nothing runs yet
    .filter { it.isNotBlank() }

emails.collect { send(it) }      // terminal: suspends per element
pitfalls: A cold flow re-runs its whole pipeline for every collector, so the transform (and any side effect in it) executes once per collection.

Concurrency is explicit: without buffer/flowOn/flatMapMerge the upstream and the transform run sequentially in the collector's context, and a blocking call inside the suspend transform blocks its thread.
An exception inside the transform cancels the whole flow and travels to the collector unless catch/retry operators are placed correctly on the chain.
